figures.caption: Compare plant height separately from pod colour. These contrasting forms give us two characteristics to follow in the offspring.
figures.alt: A tall pea plant on the left and a short plant beside it, with a separate upper-right inset showing a green pod on the left and a yellow pod on the right.
figures.introductionAndViewingText: Look first at the two contrasts below. Compare the height of the plant on the left with the smaller plant beside it. Then look at the pods in the upper-right inset: green on the left and yellow on the right. Height and pod colour are separate characteristics, even though one plant has both.
figures.followingExplanation: We can name four possible combinations of these appearances: tall with green pods, tall with yellow pods, short with green pods, and short with yellow pods. Each combination describes a phenotype, the observed characteristics. The picture alone does not tell us which combinations a particular cross will produce or how frequent they will be. For that, we need to know the parents and follow their allele contributions.
figures.teachingQuestion: Why track height and pod colour in the same plants?
figures.featureAndMeaning: The two plant heights and the green-left/yellow-right pod inset; no cross or genotype is depicted.

figures.caption: The starting cross uses tall, green-pod and short, yellow-pod breeding lines. Their known breeding history supplies information beyond the appearances in the picture.
figures.alt: The chosen P plants: a tall plant with green pods on the left crossed with a short plant with yellow pods on the right. Boxed pod details enlarge the colour contrast.
figures.introductionAndViewingText: The drawing below shows the chosen parents. Read the left plant's height and its enlarged pod together, then do the same for the right plant. The outlined boxes and connecting lines enlarge the pods so their colours can be compared; they do not show offspring.
figures.followingExplanation: Use T and t for the height gene's alleles, and G and g for the pod-colour gene's alleles. An allele is a version of a gene. A locus is that gene's position on a chromosome. Different letters keep the two loci separate; uppercase and lowercase forms of the same letter identify versions at one locus.
figures.teachingQuestion: Which known lines form the P cross?
figures.featureAndMeaning: Tall/green parent left, short/yellow right, pod callouts; breeding history supplies genotype information.

figures.caption: Different choices between identical allele copies repeat the same gamete label: TTGG contributes TG and ttgg contributes tg.
figures.alt: Combination arrows around TTGG give TG, TG, TG, TG. Arrows around ttgg give tg, tg, tg, tg. Each repeated list contains only one distinct gamete type.
figures.introductionAndViewingText: Use the arrows in the next image to follow one height letter and one pod-colour letter from each parent. Then inspect the lists beneath them. The repeated TG labels on the left all name the same distinct gamete type. The repeated tg labels on the right also name just one type.
figures.followingExplanation: There are many physical gametes, but only one distinct allele combination from each parent at these two loci. TG has probability 1 from TTGG, and tg has probability 1 from ttgg. Joining them restores a pair at each locus: T with t gives Tt, and G with g gives Gg. Every available combination is therefore TtGg.
figures.teachingQuestion: Which distinct contribution can each homozygous P parent supply?
figures.featureAndMeaning: Repeated TG and tg are redundant labels of one distinct type per parent; arrows enumerate combinations rather than depict meiosis.

figures.caption: The repeated cells show the same F1 result. One TG-by-tg cell would include the only distinct contribution pair in this starting cross.
figures.alt: An expanded P-cross grid repeats TG in all four columns and tg in all four rows. Every cell is TtGg. Its annotation identifies all F1 offspring as heterozygous at both loci, tall with green pods.
figures.introductionAndViewingText: The resulting plants are the F1 generation, the offspring of the P cross. Look at the expanded display below. Read a TG label across the top and a tg label down the side, then follow them to their shared cell. Repeat that reading at another position and notice why the genotype does not change.
figures.followingExplanation: The sixteen drawn cells do not represent sixteen different genotypes or a requirement to grow sixteen offspring. Repeating identical row and column labels has expanded the display without adding a new possibility. With each parental contribution certain, the one distinct pairing has probability 1 × 1 = 1.
figures.teachingQuestion: Why are all F1 offspring TtGg?
figures.featureAndMeaning: Four identical row and column labels give16identical cells; the one distinct pairing is certain.

figures.caption: F2 includes four phenotype combinations. The diagram gives their 9:3:3:1 model expectation; it is not a photograph or a counted set of sixteen plants.
figures.alt: The complete TtGg by TtGg F2 grid has TG, Tg, tG and tg on both edges. Green ovals mark nine tall green-pod cells, yellow ovals three tall yellow-pod cells, green rectangles three short green-pod cells, and a yellow rectangle one short yellow-pod cell. The 9:3:3:1 ratio is already printed at right.
figures.introductionAndViewingText: Now examine the F2 diagram. Its whole grid and ratio are visible. Begin with the legend on the right: oval outlines mark tall plants, rectangular outlines mark short plants, and green or yellow outlines identify pod colour. Use those two features together to find the four phenotype groups before trying to explain the number of cells in each group.
figures.followingExplanation: The tall/green and short/yellow appearances of the original parents are present, but F2 also includes tall/yellow and short/green. Those combinations were absent from the selected P parents. The height and pod-colour forms have been brought together in new ways.
figures.teachingQuestion: What phenotype combinations need explaining in F2?
figures.featureAndMeaning: Tall ovals, short rectangles, green/yellow outlines; ratio is fully visible; original static display is not raw counts.

figures.caption: Compare the two top orientations, then trace the long and short chromosomes into the lower cells. The two possibilities represent alternatives across meioses, not consecutive stages of one meiosis.
figures.alt: Two alternative orientations of long and short homologous chromosome pairs. The long pair retains its arrangement while the short pair reverses. Homologues separate into the middle cells, labelled Metaphase II; sisters then separate, producing four labelled chromosome-combination types across the two alternatives.
figures.introductionAndViewingText: At metaphase I, homologous pairs line up before separating. The direction faced by one pair does not determine the direction faced by another pair. The image below lets us compare that difference. Start with the two top cells labelled Possibility 1 and Possibility 2. Keep the long red/blue pair in view, then notice that the short pair reverses its arrangement.
figures.followingExplanation: Follow Possibility 1 down to the middle cells. One cell receives the two blue homologues and the other receives the two red homologues. Under Possibility 2, each middle cell instead receives one blue and one red homologue. The colours distinguish the chromosome origins in this schematic. They do not mean dominant and recessive, and the image does not print T, t, G or g on the chromosomes.
figures.teachingQuestion: How can different homologous pairs produce independent combinations?
figures.featureAndMeaning: Long pair retains arrangement while short reverses; top metaphase I, middle Metaphase II, bottom repeated combination classes; colour denotes origin, not dominance.

figures.caption: Follow each branch from AaBb through one allele at the first locus and one at the second. Each endpoint is one haploid gamete, with probability one quarter. Schematic — not to scale.
figures.alt: Follow each branch from AaBb through one allele at the first locus and one at the second. Each endpoint is one haploid gamete, with probability one quarter.
figures.introductionAndViewingText: The small circles along the bottom are location labels A, B, C and D. Their job differs from the allele letters in the larger branch circles. For example, follow allele A and then allele b. The endpoint is location B, and the bottom key reads “B · Ab”: location B represents gamete Ab. Use that key when reading the other endpoints.
figures.followingExplanation: The arrows organize possibilities; they do not show a chromosome splitting into four parts or two parents joining. Each full path has probability ½ × ½ = ¼ in this model. Returning to the peas, the same reasoning produced TG, Tg, tG and tg. The chromosome orientations explain why the two choices can be independent; the branch diagram helps us list them without omissions.
figures.teachingQuestion: How does each branch path represent one allele from each locus?
figures.featureAndMeaning: Large A/a and B/b circles name alleles; small bottom A/B/C/D circles name locations. Locked mapping A→AB, B→Ab, C→aB, D→ab.
